cues.text: The King's Closest Friend
Born in London around 1118 to a family of Norman merchant stock, Thomas received a solid education.
He later entered the household of Archbishop Theobald of Canterbury, who recognized his evident talent and recommended him to the young King Henry II as chancellor in 1155.
As chancellor, Thomas became, by the near-unanimous testimony of contemporary chroniclers, Henry's closest companion and most trusted servant.
He lived in splendor that rivaled the royal court itself and rode at the king's side in military campaigns.
He executed the king's policies with such loyalty and competence that, by his mid-thirties, he was arguably the most powerful subject in all of Henry's wide territories.
A Transformation No One Expected
When Archbishop Theobald died in 1161, Henry, anticipating future conflicts between crown and Church, engineered Thomas's election as the new Archbishop of Canterbury .
Confident that his loyal chancellor would continue serving royal interests in this ecclesiastical role, Henry dismissed Thomas's warning that the appointment would end their friendship.
Thomas's prediction proved entirely accurate.
Almost immediately upon his consecration, Thomas underwent a genuine and thoroughgoing transformation, resigning the chancellorship.
He adopted a life of personal austerity in place of his former luxury, committing himself with the same total intensity he had once given to royal service.
He defended the rights and liberties of the Church against the very crown he had previously served so faithfully.
A Conflict Over Who Judges the Clergy
The central conflict between Thomas and Henry crystallized around the Constitutions of Clarendon , a set of royal customs Henry sought to impose in 1164.

These customs would have subjected clergy accused of crimes to trial in royal rather than Church courts — a direct challenge, in Thomas's judgment, to the Church's God-given independence from secular control.
Thomas refused to accept these constitutions despite mounting royal pressure.
As the conflict escalated into direct confrontation, he fled England in 1164 rather than submit.
This began a six-year exile in France, during which he continued, through correspondence and appeals to the pope, to resist the king's encroachments on the Church's liberty.
A Fragile Peace, Quickly Broken
After years of failed negotiation, a fragile reconciliation was patched together in 1170, and Thomas returned to England.
He immediately excommunicated several bishops who had participated in a coronation ceremony for Henry's son, which Thomas regarded as a further usurpation of his own archiepiscopal rights.
News of these excommunications reached Henry, then in Normandy, and provoked an outburst of fury from the frustrated king against his former friend.
Four knights present at court took these words, whether accurately or not, as an implicit royal command.
Murdered at the Altar

On 29 December 1170, four knights — William de Tracy, Reginald Fitz-Urse, Hugh de Morville, and Richard le Breton — arrived at Canterbury Cathedral and confronted Thomas, demanding he lift the excommunications and submit to the king.

When Thomas refused, standing his ground rather than fleeing the church, the knights struck him down with their swords in a side chapel of his own cathedral, killing him before the altar he had spent his archiepiscopate defending.
Legacy
The shock of Thomas's murder reverberated across all of Christendom.
Though he had given no direct order for the killing, Henry II performed public penance for creating the climate that produced it.
He walked barefoot through Canterbury's streets and submitted to ritual scourging by the cathedral's monks.
Canonized within three years of his death, Thomas Becket's shrine at Canterbury became one of medieval Europe's most visited pilgrimage destinations.
Chaucer later immortalized it in his Canterbury Tales .

Eight and a half centuries later, his martyrdom remains one of Christian history's most vivid and enduring testimonies to the Church's insistence that its own freedom belongs to God alone, and to no earthly throne.
